opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to how tightly the pieces are actually coupled once you move from single-turn chat to long-horizon agentic work.

When you assemble an agent framework out of models from different sources, say one model for planning, another for coding, a third for retrieval or tool calls, each of them was trained with its own assumptions: its own formatting habits, its own way of expressing uncertainty, its own idea of what a "good" intermediate step looks like. In a short task you barely notice. But in an agent loop that runs for dozens or hundreds of steps, those small mismatches compound. One model hands off something slightly off-distribution for the next one, that one compensates in a slightly weird way, and after enough steps the whole trajectory drifts. You end up spending a lot of engineering effort on glue: prompts, parsers, retries, guardrails. That glue is brittle.

When the models are trained in the same ecosystem, and especially when the agentic behavior itself is part of training, through RL on real multi-step environments, the model learns from the start how its own outputs will be consumed. It learns the tool interfaces, the context management, when to stop and verify, how to recover from its own mistakes. The capability isn't bolted on afterward. It's internalized. That's very hard to replicate by stitching together external components, because you can't backpropagate through someone else's model or run RL across a pipeline you don't control.

The second reason is the data flywheel. If you own the whole stack, every agent trajectory, every failure, every user correction becomes training signal for the next version. A framework that assembles third-party models can collect logs, but it can't close the loop into the weights. Over time that difference accumulates. It's not a one-time gap, it's a growth-rate gap.

And third, the frontier is moving toward longer tasks and more autonomy. The longer the horizon, the more the end-to-end consistency matters relative to raw per-step intelligence. A slightly weaker but coherent, jointly-optimized system can beat a collection of individually stronger parts that don't quite understand each other.

So I don't think assembled frameworks disappear. They're great for prototyping and for niche workflows. But for general, robust agents, I expect vertically integrated training, where model and agent behavior co-evolve, to pull ahead more and more clearly.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the widening gap to coherence, long-horizon performance, and a data flywheel, but does not frame the comparison as depending on the product of effectiveness, cost, and efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the gap will widen because the two approaches are fundamentally different things, even though they look similar from the outside.

When you assemble models in an agent framework, you're essentially gluing together components that were never trained to work with each other. Each model was optimized for its own objective, with its own data distribution, its own way of representing intent and uncertainty. You then connect them through prompts and text interfaces, and hope that the information passes through cleanly. In practice, every handoff loses something. The planner doesn't really know what the executor is good at. The executor can't tell the planner that a step is ambiguous. You end up writing a lot of scaffolding code to patch over these mismatches, and that scaffolding is brittle. It works for the demo, and then it breaks when the task shifts slightly.

Models trained in the same ecosystem don't have this problem in the same way. When the pretraining, the post-training, the tool-use data, and the evaluation are all designed together, the model learns the whole workflow end to end. It learns when to call a tool and when not to, how to read the tool's output, how to recover when something fails. That behavior is in the weights, not in a wrapper. And crucially, every time the base model gets better, that whole capability gets better with it, because the training signal flows through the entire chain.

The reason I say the gap becomes more significant rather than staying constant is that tasks are getting longer. For a three-step task, the loss at each interface is small, and a framework can compensate. For a task with fifty or a hundred steps, those small losses compound. A system where the parts genuinely share representations and were optimized jointly degrades much more gracefully over long horizons than one held together by prompt engineering.

There's also a data flywheel aspect. If you control the whole stack, every interaction becomes training data for the next generation, and the improvements go directly back into the model. If you're assembling other people's models, you're stuck at the application layer. You can tune prompts and routing, but you can't change the underlying behavior. Over time, the people who can train end to end accumulate an advantage that the framework builders simply can't close from the outside.

So I don't think agent frameworks disappear. They're very useful for getting started and for experimenting. But for the hardest, longest, most reliable agentic work, I expect native integration to pull further and further ahead.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the widening gap to joint training, compounding handoff losses, and a data flywheel. It does not frame the comparison as depending on the product of effectiveness, cost, and efficiency.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is whether the models learn to work together, or whether we’re connecting them after training. In an agent framework, you can define roles, pass messages, and route tasks between different models. But each model may have different assumptions about what information to provide, when to ask for help, and what counts as completing a task. The framework has to bridge those differences.

Within the same ecosystem, there’s an opportunity to train that collaboration directly: how to delegate, what context to share, and how to recover when another model makes a mistake. You can optimize for the result of the whole system, rather than just the capability of each individual model.

As tasks get longer and require more coordination, those small differences at each handoff can accumulate. That’s why I’d expect the gap to grow—provided the shared ecosystem actually uses that opportunity to train the models together. Simply having the same model provider isn’t enough.

r001.rationale: The response attributes a growing gap to collaboration training, coordination, and handoff differences. It does not frame the comparison in terms of the combined effectiveness, cost, and efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect it to become more significant because an agent’s performance depends on how well the models work together, not just how capable each model is individually. When you assemble models from different sources, the framework has to bridge differences in how they interpret instructions, represent context, and pass results to one another. Each handoff can lose information or introduce errors, and those problems compound as tasks become longer.

Models trained within the same ecosystem can be optimized for those interactions. They can learn what information another component needs, when to delegate, and how to recover when something goes wrong. So the advantage is potentially deeper than better integration: it’s coordination learned during training. As agents take on more complex work, I expect that coordination to matter increasingly.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes coordination and performance as tasks grow more complex, but does not frame the comparison in terms of the product of effectiveness, cost, and efficiency.
